mechanism: HELM structures evaluation as a cross-product of scenarios × metrics × models, then mandates dense coverage: every model is benchmarked on every core scenario under standardized prompting conditions, and every scenario is measured on 7 metrics simultaneously (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency). Sparse prior evaluation allowed models to be selectively reported on favorable scenarios, hiding trade-offs. Forced density causally exposes inter-metric and inter-scenario trade-offs that selective benchmarking structurally conceals.
invariant: When evaluation coverage is sparse and self-selected, reported performance systematically overstates true capability breadth. Mandating dense, standardized co-evaluation across all conditions is necessary to reveal trade-offs that selective reporting suppresses — regardless of domain or model family.
prediction: Models that rank highly on accuracy-only leaderboards will rank materially lower when calibration, fairness, and toxicity are jointly considered. Specifically, no single model should Pareto-dominate all others across all 7 metrics, and accuracy rank should be a poor predictor of fairness or robustness rank.
failure_mode: When the scenario taxonomy itself is incomplete — e.g. question answering for neglected English dialects or trustworthiness metrics are absent — dense coverage of the chosen scenarios still yields a systematically biased picture, and the multi-metric structure provides false confidence in holism.
source_excerpt: Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on a set of core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions.
